text.p: Penguin colonies in some parts of Antarctica have dwindled by up to 40 percent in the past two decades due to global warming, the environmental group Greenpeace said on Tuesday.

Receding glaciers and heavier snow caused by rising temperatures have disrupted breeding patterns of the small Adelie penguins, whose population near the U.S. Palmer Station scientific base has fallen to 9,200 couples from 15,200 in 1975, Greenpeace said in a statement.
It said 21 penguin colonies had disappeared in the area.

The penguins breed in elevated rock formations that do not trap snow or water during the yearly ice meltdown. But because temperatures have risen for the past 40 years, pack ice is thinning and causing heavier snowfall, which covers nesting sites longer into the breeding season, Greenpeace said.

"In the last 40 years the lack of winters with enough pack ice has probably been an important factor for the drop in Adelie penguin populations," Greenpeace quoted U.S. scientist William Fraser as saying.
In the past 50 years Antarctica has had a temperature rise of 2.5 degrees centigrade compared to a global temperature rise of 0.5 degrees between 1860 and 1996, Greenpeace said.
Adelie penguins are the most common breed in Antarctica.
